title: Productivity and Costs, Second Quarter 2026, Revised (USDL 26-1434)
date_evidence: Transmission of material in this release is embargoed until 8:30 a.m. (ET) Thursday, September 3, 2026; Last Modified Date: September 03, 2026
key_claim: In Q2 2026 nonfarm business output rose 1.7% on 0.3% more hours (productivity +1.4%); hourly compensation rose 2.6% but real hourly compensation fell 3.3%; the labour share of output was 52.8%, the lowest in a series that begins in Q1 1947; nonfinancial corporate unit profits rose at a 43.0% annualised rate, the highest since Q2 2021.
frame_summary: A statistical release with no analytical frame beyond the arithmetic: output and profits grew faster than hours and real pay, and the labour share set a series low.
verbatim_quote: Real hourly compensation, which takes into account consumer prices, decreased 3.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026 and decreased 0.1 percent over the last four quarters. The labor share, which is the percentage of output that accrues to workers in the form of compensation, was 52.8 percent in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest level in the series, which begins in the first quarter of 1947.
verbatim_list: Nonfarm business sector labor productivity increased 1.4 percent in the second quarter of 2026, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today, as output increased 1.7 percent and hours worked increased 0.3 percent.

Unit labor costs in the nonfarm business sector increased 1.2 percent in the second quarter of 2026, reflecting a 2.6-percent increase in hourly compensation and a 1.4-percent increase in productivity.

Unit profits of nonfinancial corporations increased at an annualized rate of 43.0 percent in the second quarter of 2026, the highest rate since the second quarter of 2021. Over the last four quarters, unit profits increased 17.8 percent, the highest rate since the fourth quarter of 2021.

title: Governor Hochul Launches FutureWorks Commission Listening Sessions as Part of Plan to Address AI Workforce Impacts Across New York
date_evidence: August 19, 2026 Albany, NY # Governor Hochul Launches FutureWorks Commission Listening Sessions
key_claim: New York's 20-member FutureWorks Commission, chaired by Tom Perez, Thasunda Brown Duckett and Molly Kinder, is tasked with identifying real-time data strategies for monitoring AI's impact and proposing policy and private-sector interventions so that workers, families and small businesses, not just large corporations, gain from AI; it will report by the end of 2026, with new measures to follow in 2027; women hold 84% of administrative back-office employment in the state.
frame_summary: The state frames AI as a distributional problem to be managed through policy and private-sector interventions so that gains are shared beyond large corporations, with worker listening sessions as the input.
verbatim_quote: The members will identify real-time data strategies for monitoring AI’s impact, and propose policy and private sector interventions to ensure New York’s workers, families and small businesses, not just large corporations, stand to gain from the potential benefits of AI. The Commission will deliver its recommendations by the end of the year.
verbatim_list: In New York, women make up an outsized 84% of employment in administrative back office roles.

The Governor also highlighted today that the Commission will deliver its recommendations by the end of the year to ensure that New York is prepared to pursue new measures in the coming year to support workers and help more New Yorkers benefit from AI.

title: AI's gains are large and rising, but unevenly shared (Rachel Yuting Fan and Ha Nguyen)
date_evidence: Rachel Yuting Fan / Ha Nguyen / 20 Aug 2026
key_claim: Using five waves of the Anthropic Economic Index, two IMF economists value the time AI currently saves at about $2.7 trillion a year, roughly 3.4% of GDP across 86 countries, up from $1.2 trillion six months earlier; the gains are concentrated in richer countries and, within countries, in higher-paid occupations, though the tilt is beginning to reverse as usage spreads.
frame_summary: The authors frame AI's realised gains as large and growing but distributed toward high-income countries and high-paid occupations, with broadening only beginning, so distribution rather than scale is the policy question.
verbatim_quote: AI’s realised value is concentrated both across countries (towards richer ones) and within countries (towards higher-paid occupations).
verbatim_list: AI is already saving time worth about$ 2.7 trillion a year, roughly 3.4% of GDP across 86 countries, up from $1.2 trillion six months earlier. But those gains are unevenly shared, concentrated in rich countries and, within countries, in the highest-paid jobs.

These figures value the time AI saves at current wages, and they cover one provider’s consumer usage, so we read them as indicative. But the direction holds across every check: AI’s gains are large, rising, and unevenly shared. AI is trickling down, but it has not yet reached the bottom.
Survey-based studies find that most firms report no measurable impact on employment or productivity so far (Yotzov et al. 2026).
notes: Tier 2 (CEPR VoxEU column by IMF economists summarising IMF Working Paper 26/147). title: These 3 Agreements Secured AI Protections for 30,000 Union Workers: Insights From Three Collective Bargaining Case Studies
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-04-09T13:05:43+00:00; Eliza McCullough, Michael George April 9, 2026
key_claim: Case studies of the Financial Services Union of Ireland, SLC-CGIL in Italy and SEIU Local 668 with the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania show unions winning AI protections for roughly 30,000 members by building on existing labour law and prior technology agreements, using patterning and impact bargaining to extend terms across units, and treating agreements in one sector as precedent for others.
frame_summary: PAI frames collective agreements as a replicable governance mechanism for AI adoption that improves outcomes for both workers and employers, with cross-sector precedent-setting as the diffusion route.
verbatim_quote: These three unions have won AI protections for their roughly 30,000 members across different industries and countries.
verbatim_list: Wins in one sector shouldn’t stay there; unions can and should use each other’s agreements as models and precedent to build on across industries.

The SEIU Local 668 case study highlighted the need to seek broad, high-level agreements to protect a wider range of workers, and use “patterning” or “impact bargaining” to extend protections across unions

title: Inside the AI protections union workers are winning
key_claim: The NewsGuild-CWA has between 85 and 90 contracts with explicit AI provisions; Politico reporters forced management into arbitration over AI tools introduced without the union's permission and management dismantled them; SAG-AFTRA and ZeniMax agreements set consent, notice and bargaining rules; union representation covers 11.2% of workers (4.4% in computer occupations, 1.1% in finance); a former FTC commissioner says union-negotiated rules could map onto federal policy.
frame_summary: Axios frames collective agreements as the strongest practical guardrail American workers have against workplace AI in the absence of Congress, and the country as a patchwork in which the represented have a say and the rest do not.
verbatim_quote: The NewsGuild currently has between 85 and 90 contracts with explicit AI provisions, Schleuss says.
verbatim_list: That amounts to just 11.2% of workers, but the rate varies drastically by industry and job.
At Politico, unionized reporters forced management into arbitration after the newsroom introduced inaccurate AI reporting tools without the union's permission. Management dismantled the tools.
Former FTC Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya notes that union-negotiated rules could easily map onto federal policy — if Congress ever finds the political will.
About 36% of education, training, and library employees are unionized. Just 4.4% of workers in computer occupations are represented by unions.
In finance, it's a mere 1.1%.

title: 'I don't think there's a floor': Workers' share of America's income is at a record low before the AI boom even begins
key_claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent and Fed Chair Warsh say the AI productivity boom will make America richer; EY-Parthenon's Gregory Daco says the productivity gains so far predate AI, that productivity growth protects margins rather than income, that margins hit a record 14.9% of GDP while the labour share fell to 52.8%, and that 50% is not a floor.
frame_summary: Fortune frames the AI boom as a distribution question ('richer for whom?'), setting official optimism against evidence that gains accrue to margins and capital owners while hiring is weak and the labour share shrinks.
verbatim_quote: Margins hit a record 14.9% of GDP, while the labor share fell to 52.8%, the lowest since the government started counting in 1947. Daco said that 50% isn’t a floor.
verbatim_list: According to Gregory Daco, the EY-Parthenon chief economist, the productivity gains that explain that divergence largely predate the AI boom. “Productivity growth protects margins, not income,” Daco wrote in a note Thursday.

But analysts are starting to wonder: richer for whom? Workers’ share of U.S. income has already fallen to its lowest level on record, while corporate profit margins keep breaking records quarter by quarter.
That doesn’t mean that the AI productivity boom will fail; it just means that it’s not immediately obvious how it boosts labor’s share. “I don’t think there’s a floor,” Daco said.
notes: Tier 3 (Fortune, AI and Labor sections). Confirmed by hand via WebFetch on 2026-09-05; the sandbox has no network egress so the automated provenance re-fetch cannot run.

title: AI, meet CBA
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-09-02T11:29:50+00:00; Sep 2, 2026 By Conor Kelley and Don McIntosh
key_claim: UC Berkeley Labor Center researcher Lisa Kresge has documented over 175 union contracts with technology guardrails; Oregon AFSCME's 2025-2027 state contract bars AI in monitoring, hiring, promotion, evaluation and discipline, requires human-in-the-loop oversight and 90 days' notice; McClatchy's June 2026 agreement bans using AI to replace staff, cut pay or hours; Kaiser Permanente's 60,000-member union alliance won a labour-management AI task force; NewsGuild members have ratified more than 50 contracts restricting newsroom AI.
frame_summary: A union-supported newspaper frames AI rollout as something imposed on workers without notice, and contract language on notice, human oversight and no-replacement as the workers' only reliable counterweight.
verbatim_quote: Lisa Kresge, senior researcher at the UC Berkeley Center for Labor Research and Education, has documented over 175 examples of union contracts that try to set guardrails for the introduction of AI.
verbatim_list: Under Oregon AFSCME’s 2025-2027 contract with the State of Oregon, state agencies are prohibited from using AI to monitor employees or using AI during hiring, promotion, worker evaluations, or discipline. The contract also requires “human-in-the-loop” oversight of any AI systems. And they’re obligated to notify the union 90 days before the implementation of any AI or automated system.

On June 29, the union announced ratification of a new agreement that bans McClatchy from using AI to replace staff, decrease pay, or reduce working hours; from forcing reporters to use AI; from publishing deepfakes or from impersonating union members without their consent or creating fake AI journalists.

At Kaiser Permanente, the 22-union 60,000-member Alliance of Health Care Unions coalition won a commitment to create a labor-management task force on technology and AI and to inform the union of any new AI technology that will be implemented for monitoring productivity or performance.
Nationally, NewsGuild members have ratified more than 50 union contracts that restrict the use of AI in newsrooms

title: Union Contracts Are Becoming HR AI Playbook (Gleb Tsipursky)
